newsitem.title: GERMANY: SOCCER-DORTMUND LOOK FOR ANOTHER PARTY ON RIVALS' PATCH.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-DORTMUND LOOK FOR ANOTHER PARTY ON RIVALS' PATCH.

text.p: It is fitting that Borussia Dortmund will be looking to clinch the biggest triumph of their history at the home ground of fierce German rivals Bayern Munich in Wednesday's European Cup final.
Dortmund have successfully taken on Germany's richest club Bayern on and off the pitch in the 1990s.

In terms of the quality of the team and the club's business, it is arguable that the Ruhr side are now on level terms with the Bavarians who dominated the German game in the 1970s and 1980s and used to be the country's main European campaigners.

It was somewhat embarrassing for Bayern fans last year when Dortmund clinched the Bundesliga title for the second consecutive year in Munich's Olympic stadium after a draw with 1860 Munich who also use the ground.
Borussia even celebrated the title in Bayern's changing rooms which are used by the away team when 1860 play at the stadium.
Even though Bayern have clinched the league crown this season, a Borussia victory over Italy's Juventus in Munich on Wednesday would be difficult for many Bavarians to swallow.

Throughout the 1990s Bayern chairman Franz Beckenbauer, who is almost certain to be in the stadium on Wednesday, has been desperate to see Bayern win the most prestigious club trophy for the first time since their three triumphs in the mid 1970s.
But in the past two seasons "the Kaiser" has had to watch his Ruhr rivals pick up the big cash from the Champions'League.
Until the 1990s when they won the title in 1995 and 1996 Dortmund were a pretty average club.
It could boast just three German championships in 1956, 1957 and 1963 and one triumph in Europe in the 1966 European Cup Winners' Cup when they beat Liverpool in a Glasgow final.
Historically, Dortmund have a long way to go before they can match Bayern's record 13 league titles.
But in the mid 1990s when money, marketing and television deals are the key elements of running a successful football club, Dortmund are major players.

Dortmund can boast just 4,500 members compared to Bayern's 49,800. But trying to buy a ticket in Borussia's Westfalenstadium for any league match is as testing as finding a German town centre without a sausage stand.
Last season Dortmund boasted average crowds of 41,886, the second highest in the league behind Bayern's 59,766.
The club have used the cash they have earned from numerous appearances in Europe in recent seasons to expand the stadium. Dortmund can fill the extra seats without trying.
Despite the unemployment problems of the industrial Ruhr the club have fanatical supporters, some of whom look to football for an escape from the harsh realities of life in the region.
The club is run with marketing flair. Walk around any shopping centre in Germany and there will be a 12-year-old wearing a bright yellow Borussia shirt.

Dortmund are all about solid sponsoring deals, marketing, guaranteed capacity crowds. Just a few years ago it would have been unthinkable that the club could have attracted Germany's big names to one of the most unattractive parts of the country.

Yet in recent years Dortmund have frustrated Bayern by buying up top internationals like libero Matthias Sammer, midfielder Andy Moeller, wing-back Stefan Reuter and defender Juergen Kohler when they returned from periods in Italy.
